nameStory: The Greater Yellowlegs gets its name from its most obvious feature - those bright yellow legs that look like they've been dipped in paint! The 'greater' part distinguishes it from its smaller cousin, the Lesser Yellowlegs, though telling them apart can be tricky even for experienced birders.
description: The Greater Yellowlegs is a tall, elegant shorebird about the size of a crow, standing roughly 14 inches high. It's dressed in mottled gray-brown plumage above with a white belly, and sports those trademark bright yellow legs that seem almost too colorful for such a subtle bird. Its long, straight bill and lanky build give it a graceful, almost heron-like appearance as it wades through shallow water. This is one of our larger sandpipers, built for reaching into deeper water than its smaller cousins.

idTips.label: Bright yellow legs
idTips.description: Unmistakable lemon-yellow legs that stand out like traffic cones against muddy backgrounds - much brighter and more obvious than the pale legs of most other shorebirds

idTips.label: Long straight bill
idTips.description: Dark, needle-straight bill that's noticeably longer than the head - about 1.5 times the head length - perfect for probing in mud and sand

idTips.label: Mottled gray-brown back
idTips.description: Upper parts look like a tweedy jacket with dark and light brown speckles creating a salt-and-pepper pattern that provides excellent camouflage

idTips.label: White rump patch
idTips.description: Distinctive white triangle on the lower back and rump that flashes conspicuously when the bird takes flight - like a built-in landing light

idTips.label: Alert, upright posture
idTips.description: Stands tall and proud with neck extended, often the first bird to spot danger and sound the alarm with loud, piercing calls

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Notably larger and more robust than most sandpipers, with a lanky, almost gangly appearance that makes it stand out in mixed flocks

habitat: Look for Greater Yellowlegs around shallow wetlands throughout New England - mudflats, salt marshes, pond edges, flooded fields, and the margins of slow-moving streams. They prefer areas where water is ankle-deep or less, allowing them to wade while probing for food. During migration, they're often found at coastal estuaries and inland sewage treatment ponds.

seasonality.spring: April through May brings migrating birds heading north to breeding grounds. Look for them in breeding plumage with more distinct markings and increased vocal activity at wetland stopover sites.
seasonality.summer: Most birds have moved on to breed in Canada and Alaska, though a few non-breeding individuals may linger at prime feeding spots throughout New England.
seasonality.fall: Peak migration runs from July through October, with adults arriving first in July followed by juveniles. Fall birds show less distinct plumage but are often more approachable than spring migrants.
seasonality.winter: Uncommon but regular winter residents along the coast and at unfrozen inland waters, where they may be found alone or in small groups continuing to feed actively.

funFact: Greater Yellowlegs are the ultimate frequent flyers of the bird world, with some individuals traveling over 6,000 miles twice a year between their Arctic breeding grounds and South American wintering areas - that's like flying from New York to Rome and back, twice every year for their entire lives!
confusionNotes: The Lesser Yellowlegs is nearly identical but smaller with a thinner, shorter bill. Memory trick: Greater Yellowlegs has a bill that's 'greater' than its head length, while Lesser Yellowlegs has a bill about equal to its head length. Greater also tends to be more wary and vocal.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sandpipers,' Greater Yellowlegs actually prefer muddy areas over sandy beaches. The name 'sandpiper' is a bit misleading for this entire family - many species are more commonly found in mud, grass, or even woodland settings than on actual sand.
compareHints: Among its Tringa relatives, Greater Yellowlegs is larger than Lesser Yellowlegs and Solitary Sandpiper, with brighter yellow legs than either. It's smaller than the chunky Willet, which has blue-gray legs and a thicker bill. The Greater's straight bill also distinguishes it from the slightly upturned bill of the Willet.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Tringa relatives, the willet dwarfs both greater and lesser yellowlegs with its robust build and lacks their bright yellow legs entirely.
Compared to its Tringa cousins, the Solitary Sandpiper is smaller than both Greater and Lesser Yellowlegs with much darker, greenish legs instead of bright yellow ones.
Compared to its close relative the Greater Yellowlegs, the Lesser is noticeably smaller with a shorter, always-straight bill.
Wood Sandpiper is much smaller and more delicate than both Greater and Lesser Yellowlegs, with proportionally shorter legs and bill.
Compared to its New England relatives in the same genus, the Common Redshank is smaller than Greater Yellowlegs but similar in size to Lesser Yellowlegs, though much stockier in build.
Compared to its New England cousins, the spotted redshank has the brightest colored legs - much more vivid red-orange than the yellow of both yellowlegs species.
